newsitem.title: USA: Clinton softens stance on budget ammendment.
newsitem.headline: Clinton softens stance on budget ammendment.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday eased his opposition to a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget -- a top Republican goal -- before a meeting with leaders of the Republican-run Congress.
The Democratic president said he could accept such an amendment if it were flexible enough to cope with a recession.
"I just want to make sure that if we have one ... it needs to clearly give us the possibility of dealing with a recession," Clinton told White House reporters.

He made public the softening of his stance only hours before he was to host congressional leaders at a post-election conciliation meeting aimed at discussing his second-term agenda -- notably his desire to balance the budget by 2002.

Since winning re-election last Tuesday in an election where voters also returned Republican majorities to both houses of Congress, Clinton has exhorted his opponents to work with him, especially on his top priority of balancing the budget.
His shift on the amendment issue seemed a bow toward the election results. Republicans gained two seats in the Senate, making the passage of such an amendment almost inevitable.
In the last Congress, the ammendment passed the Republican House of Representatives overwhelmingly, but failed by one vote in the Senate.
At the time, Clinton derided the amendment as a "gimmick."
"My problems with a constitutional ammendment were always more a question of how to manage the larger economic problems of the country," he said on Tuesday.
"We don't want to wind up with a Congress some day in a recession raising taxes or throwing unemployed people off health care because we're trying to reach a balanced budget.
"You could actually wind up making the deficit worse."

Clinton repeated his appeal to congressional Republicans to meet him halfway, adding a slight edge to his comments by saying the election outcome was an unmistakeable signal voters want collaboration between the two parties.

"There is no way to read the election results as they came out as a repudiation of the last two months of the last Congress. It clearly has to be seen as a ratification of the last two months of the last Congress," Clinton said, alluding to the wave of legislation passed before the election.
"I'm not always as quick on the uptake as I ought to be, but it shouldn't take another year and a half to figure that out," he said.
The federal budget has been the major battleground between the two parties since the Republicans regained control of both houses of Congress in the 1994 mid-term elections.

The deficit had exploded to nearly $300 billion by 1992 when Clinton was first elected. It has been trimmed to about $107 billion under his stewardship but is expected to rise again unless further action is taken.
A stalemate over how to reduce the deficit led to two deeply unpopular government shutdowns in the last year, with voters blaming the Republicans both times.
Both sides are now under pressure to see if they can work together or will return to partisan struggle.
Republican Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott signalled on Sunday that he still has some bones to pick with Clinton.
On NBC's Meet the Press, Lott said Clinton had been "irresponsible" in portraying the Republican position on the Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

Many analysts say cutting Medicare costs is one key to controlling federal deficits and restoring vitality to the programme itself, but Clinton claimed the Republican proposals were too severe and would victimise low-income retirees.
"On Medicare, he's been irresponsible, he's misled the people, he's misinformed them (elderly voters)," Lott said of Clinton's campaign claims. "It's been disingenuous."

On Tuesday, Clinton did not appear sympathetic to Lott's concern. "There is no point in us going back and litigating what we thought of each other's programmes that we didn't agree with," he said. "In the end, we will still have to reconcile."
"We need to focus on how we can reach agreement now. We are in this boat together and we have to paddle it together. That's what the American people want," Clinton said.
